stem: A Pod declares an `emptyDir` volume shared by its two containers. One container crashes and the kubelet restarts it. What happens to the files in the `emptyDir`?

options.text: They are wiped, because every container restart recreates its volumes from scratch
options.why: Volumes belong to the Pod, not the container, so a container restart does not reset them.

options.text: They survive, because an emptyDir lives as long as the Pod stays on that node
options.why: An emptyDir is created when the Pod is assigned to a node and removed only when the Pod is removed.

options.text: They are copied into a PersistentVolume so the restarted container can find them
options.why: emptyDir is never backed by a PersistentVolume; it uses node-local storage or RAM.

options.text: They survive only if the volume sets `medium: Memory` instead of the node disk
options.why: The medium changes where data is stored, not how long it lives; both kinds survive container restarts.

explanation: An `emptyDir` volume is created when the Pod is scheduled to a node and deleted when the Pod is removed from that node. Container crashes and restarts inside the Pod keep the data, which makes emptyDir useful as scratch space or for sharing files between containers in the same Pod. It is not durable: if the Pod is deleted or rescheduled elsewhere, the data is gone.

stem: True or false: a PersistentVolumeClaim with access mode `ReadWriteOnce` can be mounted by only one Pod at a time.

options.text: True
options.why: It is a common belief, but ReadWriteOnce restricts the volume to one node, not one Pod.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: ReadWriteOnce allows a single node to mount the volume read-write, and several Pods on that node can use it.

explanation: ReadWriteOnce (RWO) means the volume can be mounted read-write by a single node. Multiple Pods scheduled on that same node can all use it. If you need to guarantee a single Pod across the whole cluster, use `ReadWriteOncePod` (RWOP), which is stable since Kubernetes 1.29 and supported only for CSI volumes.

stem: Which statement best describes the split between a PersistentVolume (PV) and a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)?

options.text: A PV is cluster storage; a PVC is a namespaced request that binds to a PV
options.why: PVs are cluster-scoped resources, and a PVC asks for size and access modes and binds to a matching PV.

options.text: A PVC is the physical disk, and the PV is the Pod-level mount pointing at it
options.why: It is the reverse: the PV represents the storage and the PVC is the user's request for it.

options.text: Both are namespaced, and a PV must live in the same namespace as its Pod
options.why: PVs are cluster-scoped; only PVCs (and Pods) live in namespaces.

options.text: A PVC is only needed for StatefulSets; Deployments mount PVs directly by name
options.why: Any Pod uses a PVC to consume a PersistentVolume; Pods do not reference PVs directly.

explanation: A PersistentVolume is a cluster-scoped resource representing real storage, provisioned by an administrator or dynamically by a StorageClass. A PersistentVolumeClaim is a namespaced request for storage of a certain size and access mode. The control plane binds each PVC to one PV, one-to-one, and Pods reference the PVC by name in their `volumes` section.

stem: Which annotation, set to `"true"` on a StorageClass, makes it the cluster's default for PVCs that omit `storageClassName`? Type the annotation key.
explanation: The annotation `storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"` marks a StorageClass as the default. A PVC that omits `storageClassName` gets this class, and dynamic provisioning creates a PV for it. If more than one class is marked default, Kubernetes uses the most recently created one.

stem: Match each PersistentVolume access mode abbreviation with its meaning.

options.text: Read-write by a single node
options.why: RWO

options.text: Read-only by many nodes
options.why: ROX

options.text: Read-write by many nodes
options.why: RWX

options.text: Read-write by a single Pod in the whole cluster
options.why: RWOP

explanation: The command-line abbreviations map to the access modes ReadWriteOnce (one node), ReadOnlyMany (many nodes, read-only), ReadWriteMany (many nodes, read-write) and ReadWriteOncePod (one Pod). A volume type only supports the modes its storage can actually provide: block devices such as cloud disks are typically RWO only, while shared filesystems such as NFS support RWX.

stem: A StorageClass does not set `reclaimPolicy`. What reclaim policy do PersistentVolumes dynamically provisioned from it get?

options.text: `Retain`, so the data is kept after the claim goes away
options.why: Retain is the default only for manually created PVs, not for dynamically provisioned ones.

options.text: `Recycle`, which scrubs the volume and returns it to the pool
options.why: Recycle is deprecated and is never a default.

options.text: `Delete`, so removing the PVC also deletes the volume
options.why: A StorageClass that omits reclaimPolicy defaults to Delete.

options.text: None: the field must be set or the class is rejected
options.why: The field is optional and has a default.

explanation: If `reclaimPolicy` is not set on a StorageClass, it defaults to `Delete`. When the PVC bound to such a PV is deleted, the PV and its backing storage asset (for example a cloud disk) are deleted too. Manually created PVs default to `Retain`. For data you cannot afford to lose, set `reclaimPolicy: Retain` on the class or patch the PV.

stem: Which two kinds of volume are deleted automatically when the Pod that uses them is deleted? (Choose two.)

options.text: An `emptyDir` volume
options.why: It exists only for the lifetime of the Pod on its node.

options.text: A generic ephemeral volume
options.why: Its PVC is owned by the Pod, so garbage collection removes it with the Pod.

options.text: A PVC created by hand and referenced by the Pod
options.why: A standalone PVC outlives the Pods that mount it.

options.text: A `hostPath` directory on the node
options.why: The node directory remains after the Pod is gone.

options.text: A PVC created from a StatefulSet `volumeClaimTemplates` entry
options.why: By default those PVCs are retained when Pods are deleted or the set is scaled down.

explanation: Ephemeral volumes follow the Pod lifecycle. `emptyDir` is removed with the Pod, and a generic ephemeral volume creates a PVC with the Pod as owner, so it is garbage-collected with the Pod. Persistent volumes deliberately outlive Pods: a hand-made PVC, a hostPath directory and StatefulSet template PVCs all stay behind.

stem: Six web Pods spread across four nodes must all write user uploads into one shared directory. Which access mode must the PersistentVolumeClaim request?

options.text: `ReadWriteOnce`, because every Pod writes and RWO allows writing
options.why: RWO limits read-write mounting to one node, so Pods on the other nodes could not mount it.

options.text: `ReadWriteMany`, backed by a shared filesystem such as NFS or EFS
options.why: Only RWX lets many nodes mount the same volume read-write.

options.text: `ReadOnlyMany`, since many nodes need the same volume at once
options.why: ROX allows many nodes but only for reading, and the Pods must write.

options.text: `ReadWriteOncePod`, so that each Pod gets its own separate writable copy
options.why: RWOP restricts the volume to one Pod; it never creates per-Pod copies.

explanation: Writers on several nodes need `ReadWriteMany`. Block storage like a typical cloud disk cannot provide it, so the StorageClass must use a shared filesystem (NFS, Amazon EFS, Azure Files, CephFS and similar). Alternatives that avoid RWX are object storage such as S3, or routing uploads through a single service.

stem:
This PVC stays `Pending` forever, even though the cluster has a default StorageClass that provisions disks normally. Why?

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: reports
spec:
  storageClassName: ""
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 20Gi
```

options.text: An empty class name tells Kubernetes to use the default class after a short delay
options.why: An explicitly empty name is not the same as omitting the field; it never selects the default.

options.text: An empty `storageClassName` requests a classless PV, so nothing is provisioned
options.why: It can bind only to existing PVs that also have no class, and there are none.

options.text: A 20Gi request exceeds the size that the default StorageClass is allowed to create
options.why: StorageClasses do not cap request sizes; the empty class name is the problem.

options.text: RWO claims always wait until a Pod mounts them, whatever the class says
options.why: Waiting for a consumer is controlled by volumeBindingMode, not by the access mode.

explanation: Setting `storageClassName: ""` is a deliberate opt-out of dynamic provisioning: the claim can only bind to pre-created PVs that have no class. Omitting the field is different, because then the default StorageClass is applied. Remove the line (or name a real class) to get a dynamically provisioned disk.

stem: A StatefulSet `db` with `volumeClaimTemplates` named `data` and default settings is scaled from 3 replicas to 1, and later back to 3. What happens to the data of `db-1` and `db-2`?

options.text: Their PVCs are kept, and the recreated Pods remount the same volumes
options.why: By default PVCs are retained on scale-down and reused by the Pod with the same ordinal.

options.text: The PVCs are deleted on scale-down, so the new Pods start with empty disks
options.why: Deleting on scale-down only happens with `whenScaled: Delete`.

options.text: The PVCs are kept but must be rebound by hand before the Pods can start
options.why: Rebinding is automatic because the PVC names follow the Pod ordinals.

options.text: Their data is merged into `db-0`'s volume when the set shrinks to one
options.why: Kubernetes never merges volumes; each ordinal keeps its own PVC.

explanation: Each ordinal gets its own PVC (`data-db-0`, `data-db-1`, `data-db-2`). With the default `persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy` (`whenDeleted: Retain`, `whenScaled: Retain`), scaling down deletes the Pods but keeps their PVCs. When the set scales up again, Pod `db-1` uses PVC `data-db-1` and finds its old data.

stem: A StatefulSet named `web` has a `volumeClaimTemplates` entry named `www`. What is the name of the PVC used by Pod `web-2`? Type the name.
explanation: StatefulSet PVCs are named `<template name>-<StatefulSet name>-<ordinal>`, so the third Pod `web-2` uses `www-web-2`. The stable name is what lets a replacement Pod with the same ordinal find the same volume after rescheduling.

stem: A Deployment with 3 replicas mounts one PVC with access mode `ReadWriteOnce` on a cloud block disk. One Pod runs; the other two are stuck in `ContainerCreating` with `Multi-Attach error for volume`. What is happening?

options.text: The disk is too small for three Pods, so the CSI driver refuses extra mounts
options.why: Capacity is not checked per Pod; the error is about attaching to more than one node.

options.text: The two Pods landed on other nodes, and an RWO disk can attach to only one node
options.why: RWO block volumes attach to a single node at a time.

options.text: RWO allows exactly one Pod, so the scheduler deliberately blocks the second and third
options.why: RWO is per node; Pods on the same node could share the volume.

options.text: The PVC is still bound to an old ReplicaSet and must be released first
options.why: PVCs are not bound to ReplicaSets; this is an attach conflict across nodes.

explanation: A cloud block disk with `ReadWriteOnce` can be attached to only one node. Replicas scheduled to other nodes cannot attach it, so they hang in `ContainerCreating` with a Multi-Attach error. Either give each replica its own volume (a StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates), use a shared RWX filesystem, or run a single replica.

stem: Your team needs to grow a PVC from 50Gi to 100Gi. Which two conditions are required? (Choose two.)

options.text: The StorageClass has `allowVolumeExpansion: true`
options.why: Expansion is only allowed for claims whose class permits it.

options.text: You raise `spec.resources.requests.storage` on the PVC
options.why: Editing the claim's request triggers the resize.

options.text: You edit `spec.capacity.storage` directly on the bound PV
options.why: Users resize through the PVC; editing the PV does not resize the disk.

options.text: You delete the PVC and create a new 100Gi one with the same name
options.why: That would provision a new, empty volume (or delete the old one).

options.text: The PVC uses access mode ReadWriteMany
options.why: Expansion does not depend on the access mode.

explanation: To expand a volume, the StorageClass must set `allowVolumeExpansion: true`, and you edit the PVC to request more storage. The volume plugin (for CSI, the external-resizer and the node plugin) grows the disk and then the filesystem. Kubernetes does not support shrinking a PVC below its current size.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Persistent Volumes (Expanding Persistent Volumes Claims)

stem: A developer wants to mount `/var/data` from the node into a Pod with `hostPath`. Which two risks should you raise? (Choose two.)

options.text: The data is tied to one node, so a rescheduled Pod sees different or no data
options.why: hostPath content lives only on the node that ran the Pod.

options.text: Host filesystem access can be used to escalate privileges or tamper with the node
options.why: Kubernetes warns that hostPath exposes privileged host resources.

options.text: hostPath volumes are wiped every time the container restarts
options.why: The node directory persists across container and Pod restarts.

options.text: hostPath counts against the Pod memory limit like a tmpfs
options.why: hostPath is a node directory, not RAM-backed storage.

options.text: hostPath is rejected by the API server unless the Pod runs as root
options.why: The API accepts it; Pod Security admission may block it, but not because of the user ID.

explanation: A `hostPath` volume mounts a file or directory from the node into the Pod. Its data is node-local, so it does not follow the Pod to another node, and it exposes the host filesystem, which can let a compromised container read secrets or modify the node. The Baseline and Restricted Pod Security Standards forbid it. Use PVCs for durable data and emptyDir for scratch space.

stem: A PVC uses a StorageClass with `volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer`. Put the events in the order they happen when a Pod that uses the claim is created.

options.text: The scheduler picks a node for the Pod
The provisioner creates a volume in that node's zone and a PV for it
The PV is bound to the PVC
The volume is attached to the node and mounted into the Pod
The containers start

explanation: With `WaitForFirstConsumer`, binding and provisioning wait until a Pod that uses the claim is scheduled. The provisioner then creates the volume where the Pod will run (respecting topology such as zones), the PV binds to the PVC, the volume is attached and mounted on the node, and only then do the containers start.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Storage Classes (Volume binding mode)

stem: True or false: you can shrink a bound PVC from 100Gi to 80Gi by lowering `spec.resources.requests.storage`, provided the filesystem has enough free space.

options.text: True
options.why: Free space does not matter: the API rejects any request below the current size.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: Kubernetes does not support shrinking a PVC to less than its current size.

explanation: Volume expansion only goes up. To get a smaller volume, create a new, smaller PVC and copy the data across (for example with a Job), then switch the workload to the new claim.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Persistent Volumes (Expanding Persistent Volumes Claims)

stem: An admin deleted a PVC whose PV has `persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain`. The PV now shows `Released`. A new PVC with the same size and class stays `Pending` instead of binding to it. Why?

options.text: Released PVs rebind automatically, but only after a 24-hour grace period ends
options.why: There is no grace period; Released PVs never rebind on their own.

options.text: The PV still holds the old claim in `spec.claimRef`, so it is not Available
options.why: Retain keeps the PV and its reference to the deleted claim until an admin clears it.

options.text: Retained PVs can only be used again by a claim with the exact same name
options.why: Even a claim with the same name will not bind while the PV is Released.

options.text: The data must first be scrubbed by Kubernetes, which `Retain` disables
options.why: Retain means Kubernetes never touches the data; reuse is a manual step.

explanation: With `Retain`, deleting the PVC leaves the PV in `Released` state with the previous claim reference intact, so it is not available for another claim. To reuse the data, remove `spec.claimRef` from the PV (or delete it and create a new PV pointing at the same storage asset); it becomes `Available` and a matching PVC, optionally with `volumeName`, can bind.

stem: A container with a 512Mi memory limit writes 400Mi of temporary files into an `emptyDir` with `medium: Memory`. Its own heap uses another 200Mi. What is the most likely outcome?

options.text: Nothing: tmpfs usage comes from node memory outside the Pod's limits
options.why: Memory-backed emptyDir usage is charged to the container that writes it.

options.text: The files spill to the node disk once tmpfs reaches 512Mi
options.why: tmpfs never spills to disk; it is RAM only.

options.text: It is OOM-killed, since tmpfs files count toward its memory limit
options.why: 400Mi of tmpfs plus 200Mi of heap exceeds the 512Mi limit.

options.text: The kubelet evicts the Pod for exceeding its ephemeral-storage request
options.why: Memory-backed emptyDir is accounted as memory, not ephemeral storage.

explanation: With `medium: Memory`, Kubernetes mounts a tmpfs, and the files written there count as memory used by the container. Here 400Mi of files plus a 200Mi heap exceeds the 512Mi limit, so the kernel OOM-kills the container. Set a `sizeLimit` on the emptyDir and size the memory limit to include it.

stem: A ConfigMap is mounted into a container with `subPath: app.conf`. After the ConfigMap is edited, the container still reads the old file indefinitely. Why?

options.text: A `subPath` mount does not receive ConfigMap updates
options.why: Only full-directory ConfigMap mounts are updated by the kubelet.

options.text: ConfigMap edits never reach running Pods until they are recreated
options.why: Directory mounts are refreshed automatically after a short delay.

options.text: The kubelet caches ConfigMaps for 24 hours before syncing
options.why: The sync period is about a minute plus cache delay, not a day.

options.text: The ConfigMap must be marked `immutable: false` to propagate
options.why: ConfigMaps are mutable by default; immutability is opt-in.

explanation: Mounted ConfigMap volumes are updated eventually, but a container that mounts a ConfigMap key with `subPath` gets a bind mount of that single file, which does not receive updates. Mount the whole ConfigMap as a directory (and point the app at the file inside it), or roll the Pods when config changes.

stem: In a three-zone cluster, a StorageClass uses `volumeBindingMode: Immediate`. A PVC is provisioned as a disk in zone `a`. The Pod using it also has a node selector for zone `c`. What happens?

options.text: The scheduler moves the disk to zone `c` before starting the Pod
options.why: Kubernetes cannot move zonal disks between zones.

options.text: The Pod stays Pending with a volume node affinity conflict
options.why: The PV can only attach in zone `a`, which conflicts with the zone `c` selector.

options.text: The Pod starts in zone `c` and reaches the disk over the network
options.why: Zonal block disks attach only to nodes in their own zone.

options.text: The PVC is re-provisioned in zone `c` automatically
options.why: A bound PVC is never re-provisioned elsewhere.

explanation: With `Immediate`, the volume is provisioned as soon as the PVC is created, before the scheduler knows where the Pod will run. A zonal disk gets node affinity for its zone, and if the Pod's other constraints point elsewhere the Pod cannot be scheduled ("volume node affinity conflict"). `WaitForFirstConsumer` delays provisioning until the Pod is scheduled, so the volume is created in a zone that satisfies all constraints.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Storage Classes (Volume binding mode)

stem: In a CSI driver deployment, which two tasks are handled by the node plugin (the DaemonSet part) rather than the controller plugin? (Choose two.)

options.text: Mounting (staging and publishing) the volume on the node where the Pod runs
options.why: NodeStage/NodePublish calls are served by the node plugin on that node.

options.text: Registering the driver with the kubelet through node-driver-registrar
options.why: The registrar sidecar runs next to the node plugin on every node.

options.text: Creating the cloud disk when a PVC is provisioned
options.why: CreateVolume is a controller call driven by the external-provisioner.

options.text: Attaching the disk to a VM through the cloud API
options.why: ControllerPublish (attach) is driven by the external-attacher in the controller.

options.text: Taking snapshots for VolumeSnapshot objects
options.why: Snapshots are created through the controller and the external-snapshotter.

explanation: A CSI driver usually runs as a controller Deployment (with sidecars such as external-provisioner, external-attacher, external-resizer and external-snapshotter calling CreateVolume, ControllerPublishVolume and so on) plus a node DaemonSet. The node plugin mounts volumes on its node through NodeStageVolume and NodePublishVolume, and node-driver-registrar registers the driver with the kubelet.
reference: Kubernetes CSI docs: Deploying a CSI Driver

stem: Match each CSI sidecar container with the Kubernetes object or event it watches to call the driver.

options.text: external-provisioner
options.why: Watches PVCs and calls CreateVolume/DeleteVolume

options.text: external-attacher
options.why: Watches VolumeAttachment objects and calls ControllerPublish

options.text: external-resizer
options.why: Watches PVC size increases and calls ControllerExpandVolume

options.text: external-snapshotter
options.why: Watches VolumeSnapshotContent and calls CreateSnapshot

prompts.text: A new PVC needs a volume
A PVC's storage request is increased

explanation: Kubernetes does not talk to CSI drivers directly from the core controllers. Small sidecars translate API objects into CSI calls: the provisioner reacts to PVCs, the attacher to VolumeAttachment objects created by the attach/detach controller, the resizer to expanded PVCs, and the snapshotter to VolumeSnapshotContent objects.

stem: A single-replica PostgreSQL Deployment uses an RWO cloud disk and the default `RollingUpdate` strategy. After an image update, the new Pod is scheduled to another node and hangs in `ContainerCreating`, while the old Pod keeps running. What is the cleanest fix?

options.text: Increase `maxSurge` so that the new Pod gets its own separate copy of the disk
options.why: Surge creates more Pods, not more disks; the shared RWO disk is still the conflict.

options.text: Switch the PVC to ReadOnlyMany so both Pods can mount it
options.why: Postgres needs to write, and the disk type would not support it anyway.

options.text: Use `Recreate` (or a StatefulSet) so the old Pod frees the disk first
options.why: Recreate stops the old Pod before starting the new one.

options.text: Delete the PVC so the new Pod can claim the disk again
options.why: Deleting the PVC can delete the disk and all the data.

explanation: RollingUpdate starts the new Pod before the old one stops. With an RWO disk attached to the old Pod's node, the new Pod on another node cannot attach it and waits forever. `strategy.type: Recreate` stops the old Pod first, releasing the disk. A StatefulSet is the more natural home for databases: it replaces Pods one at a time and keeps a stable volume per ordinal.

stem: A cleanup script runs `kubectl delete pvc --all -n analytics`. The PVs came from a StorageClass with no `reclaimPolicy` set. What happens to the data?

options.text: The PVs and their backing disks are deleted, so the data is gone
options.why: Dynamic PVs default to Delete, which removes the storage asset.

options.text: The PVs move to Released and the data stays until an admin cleans up
options.why: That would be Retain behaviour, which is not the default here.

options.text: Nothing, because PVCs cannot be deleted while their namespace exists
options.why: PVCs can be deleted at any time; protection only delays it while Pods use them.

options.text: The disks are kept but detached, and new PVCs reattach them by name
options.why: Delete removes the disk itself, not just the attachment.

explanation: Dynamically provisioned PVs inherit their StorageClass's reclaim policy, which defaults to `Delete`. Deleting the PVC deletes the PV and the underlying disk. To protect important data, use a StorageClass with `reclaimPolicy: Retain`, patch existing PVs to Retain, and take snapshots or backups.

stem: You run `kubectl delete pvc logs-claim` while a running Pod still mounts it. The command returns, but the PVC shows `Terminating` for hours. Why?

options.text: The PV reclaim policy is Retain, so this claim can never be deleted at all
options.why: Reclaim policy affects the PV after deletion, not whether the PVC can be deleted.

options.text: The `kubernetes.io/pvc-protection` finalizer waits until no Pod uses it
options.why: Storage object in use protection delays removal while a Pod mounts it.

options.text: The CSI driver is still copying the data to a snapshot first
options.why: Deleting a PVC does not trigger snapshots.

options.text: PVCs are deleted only by the garbage collector once a day
options.why: Deletion is immediate once the finalizer is removed.

explanation: Storage Object in Use Protection adds the `kubernetes.io/pvc-protection` finalizer to PVCs. If you delete a PVC that a Pod is using, it stays `Terminating` until no Pod uses it, which prevents data loss for running workloads. Delete or move the Pod and the PVC finishes deleting. PVs have a similar `kubernetes.io/pv-protection` finalizer.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Persistent Volumes (Storage Object in Use Protection)

stem: A PVC requests `10Gi`, `ReadWriteOnce` and `storageClassName: fast`, with a label selector `tier: gold`. Which three conditions must a pre-created PV meet to bind to it? (Choose three.)

options.text: Its `storageClassName` is `fast`
options.why: Claims bind only to PVs of the requested class.

options.text: Its capacity is at least 10Gi and it supports ReadWriteOnce
options.why: Size must be enough and the access mode must be offered.

options.text: It carries the label `tier: gold`
options.why: A selector restricts binding to PVs with matching labels.

options.text: It lives in the same namespace as the PVC
options.why: PVs are cluster-scoped and have no namespace.

options.text: Its name is the same as the PVC's name
options.why: Names do not need to match; `volumeName` is optional and goes on the PVC.

options.text: Its capacity is exactly 10Gi, with no extra space
options.why: A larger PV can satisfy the claim; the extra space is simply allocated.

explanation: The binder matches a claim to a PV whose class equals the claim's class, whose capacity is at least the request, whose access modes include the requested ones, and whose labels satisfy any selector. A bigger PV can bind (the claim then sees the larger capacity). PVs are cluster-scoped, and binding is one-to-one.

stem: Which manifest restores a VolumeSnapshot named `orders-snap` into a new volume?

options.text: A VolumeSnapshotContent with `source.volumeHandle` set to the PVC name
options.why: VolumeSnapshotContent represents a snapshot, not a restored volume.

options.text: A PersistentVolume whose `claimRef` names `orders-snap`
options.why: claimRef binds a PV to a PVC, not to a snapshot.

options.text: A PVC with `dataSource: {kind: VolumeSnapshot, name: orders-snap}`
options.why: Restores provision a new volume pre-populated from the snapshot.

options.text: A VolumeSnapshotClass with `restoreFrom: orders-snap`
options.why: There is no restoreFrom field; classes only configure snapshot creation.

explanation: To restore, create a new PVC whose `dataSource` references the VolumeSnapshot (`apiGroup: snapshot.storage.k8s.io`). The CSI driver provisions a fresh volume pre-populated with the snapshot data. The snapshot and the new PVC must be in the same namespace, and the requested size must be at least the snapshot's restore size.

stem: Pods that mount a 2 TB volume with millions of files take 20 minutes to start. The Pod spec sets `securityContext.fsGroup: 2000`. What change most directly fixes the slow start?

options.text: Remove `fsGroup` and run the container as root instead
options.why: It works around the symptom but weakens security for no reason.

options.text: Set `fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch`
options.why: Ownership is then changed only if the root directory does not already match.

options.text: Mount the volume read-only so permissions are not checked
options.why: The app presumably needs to write, and read-only mounts skip only some work.

options.text: Move the data into an `emptyDir` with a larger sizeLimit
options.why: emptyDir is not persistent and would lose the data.

explanation: With `fsGroup`, the kubelet by default recursively changes ownership and permissions of every file on each mount, which is slow on large volumes. `fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch` skips the walk when the root directory already has the expected ownership and permissions. Some CSI drivers can also apply fsGroup at mount time (delegated fsGroup), avoiding the walk entirely.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Configure a Security Context (fsGroupChangePolicy)

stem:
A StatefulSet sets:

```yaml
persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy:
  whenDeleted: Retain
  whenScaled: Delete
```

It scales from 5 to 3 replicas, and later the node running `db-0` fails and `db-0` is recreated on another node. Which PVCs are deleted?

options.text: None, because `whenDeleted: Retain` overrides the scaling rule
options.why: The two settings apply to different events and don't override each other.

options.text: All five, because Delete applies whenever a Pod goes away
options.why: Rescheduling a Pod for other reasons does not count as scaling down.

options.text: Only `data-db-3` and `data-db-4`, the scaled-down ordinals
options.why: whenScaled deletes PVCs of scaled-down ordinals only.

options.text: `data-db-3`, `data-db-4` and `data-db-0`, since `db-0` was deleted
options.why: A Pod deleted by node failure keeps its PVC; only scale-down triggers deletion.

explanation: With `whenScaled: Delete`, only the PVCs belonging to ordinals removed by a scale-down are deleted, after their Pods are deleted. A Pod deleted and recreated for any other reason, such as a node failure, keeps its PVC. `whenDeleted` covers deleting the whole StatefulSet, which is Retain here.

stem: Which `volumeBindingMode` value on a StorageClass delays binding and provisioning of a PV until a Pod that uses the PVC is created? Type the value.
explanation: `WaitForFirstConsumer` lets the scheduler choose the node first, so the volume is provisioned in a topology (for example a zone) that satisfies the Pod's constraints such as node selectors, affinity and taints. The default, `Immediate`, provisions as soon as the PVC is created. Local volumes need WaitForFirstConsumer.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Storage Classes (Volume binding mode)

stem: After you raise a PVC from 100Gi to 200Gi, its capacity still shows 100Gi and its conditions include `FileSystemResizePending`. What does that indicate?

options.text: The resize failed, so the PVC must be deleted and recreated
options.why: This condition is a normal intermediate state, not a failure.

options.text: The disk grew; the filesystem grows when a Pod mounts the volume
options.why: Offline resize finishes when a Pod mounts or remounts the volume.

options.text: The StorageClass lacks `allowVolumeExpansion`, so the request is queued
options.why: Without that flag, the request would be rejected outright.

options.text: The cluster is waiting for an admin to approve the size change
options.why: Volume expansion has no approval step.

explanation: Expansion happens in two stages: the controller grows the backing volume, then the node grows the filesystem. `FileSystemResizePending` means the first stage succeeded and the filesystem resize is waiting for the node, which happens when a Pod mounts the volume. Drivers that support online expansion finish it while the Pod runs; others need the Pod restarted.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Persistent Volumes (Resizing an in-use PersistentVolumeClaim)

stem: True or false: with access mode `ReadWriteOncePod`, two Pods on the same node can still mount the same PVC.

options.text: True
options.why: That describes ReadWriteOnce, which is scoped to a node.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: ReadWriteOncePod ensures only one Pod across the whole cluster can use the PVC.

explanation: `ReadWriteOncePod` (stable since 1.29, CSI volumes only) restricts a PVC to a single Pod. A second Pod that tries to use it fails to schedule. It's useful when the application must be the only writer, which `ReadWriteOnce` cannot guarantee because RWO allows every Pod on the same node.

stem: Your team uses `local` PersistentVolumes on fast NVMe disks. Which statement is true about them?

options.text: They are provisioned dynamically by the built-in local plugin like cloud disks
options.why: Local PVs are created statically or by an external provisioner, not by a built-in one.

options.text: They need node affinity, and Pods using them are pinned to that node
options.why: The data exists only on that node, so the scheduler must place Pods there.

options.text: They survive a node failure because Kubernetes replicates them to another node
options.why: Nothing replicates them; losing the node loses access to the data.

options.text: They should use `volumeBindingMode: Immediate` so binding happens early
options.why: Local volumes should use WaitForFirstConsumer so binding considers Pod constraints.

explanation: `local` volumes represent disks attached to a specific node. The PV must set `nodeAffinity`, and Pods that use it are scheduled to that node only. Use a StorageClass with `WaitForFirstConsumer` so the scheduler can weigh the volume together with the Pod's other constraints. If the node fails, the data is unavailable, so the application must handle replication itself.

stem: You need to change `volumeClaimTemplates` in a running StatefulSet to request larger volumes. `kubectl apply` fails with a "Forbidden: updates to statefulset spec ... are forbidden" error. What is a safe approach?

options.text: Add `--force` to `kubectl apply` so the API accepts the template change
options.why: `--force` deletes and recreates the StatefulSet, which can also delete Pods abruptly.

options.text: Resize each PVC, then re-create the set after a `--cascade=orphan` delete
options.why: Orphaning keeps Pods and PVCs while the StatefulSet object is replaced.

options.text: Scale to zero, edit the template and scale back so the PVCs are reprovisioned
options.why: Scale-down keeps the PVCs by default, so their size does not change.

options.text: Delete the PVCs so the StatefulSet creates larger ones from the new template
options.why: Deleting PVCs (with Delete reclaim) destroys the data.

explanation: Most fields of a StatefulSet spec, including `volumeClaimTemplates`, are immutable. A common procedure is: resize each existing PVC (the class must allow expansion), delete the StatefulSet with `kubectl delete sts <name> --cascade=orphan` so Pods and PVCs keep running, then apply the StatefulSet with the updated template so future ordinals get the larger size. The new StatefulSet adopts the orphaned Pods.

stem: Your company wants to run a highly available PostgreSQL cluster on Kubernetes. Which two practices are sound? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use an operator (for example CloudNativePG) that handles failover and replicas
options.why: Operators encode database-specific failover, backup and upgrade logic.

options.text: Add a PodDisruptionBudget so voluntary disruptions never take down the quorum
options.why: PDBs stop node drains from evicting too many replicas at once.

options.text: Put all replicas on one ReadWriteMany volume so they share the data directory
options.why: Database replicas need their own data directories; sharing one corrupts data.

options.text: Store data in `emptyDir` and rely on replication to recover it
options.why: Losing several Pods at once would lose all copies.

options.text: Use `hostPath` on each node so data survives Pod restarts
options.why: hostPath ties data to nodes without any scheduling or failover guarantees.

explanation: Stateful databases on Kubernetes work best with an operator (CloudNativePG, Zalando, Crunchy and others) that manages replication, failover, backups and upgrades on top of StatefulSets or its own controllers. Each replica gets its own persistent volume, PodDisruptionBudgets protect quorum during node maintenance, and backups go off-cluster. A managed database service is often simpler still.
reference: Kubernetes docs: StatefulSets; Pod Disruption Budgets

stem: A batch Pod needs 200Gi of fast scratch space that should disappear with the Pod. Nodes have small local disks, but the cluster has a CSI StorageClass for network SSDs. Which option fits best?

options.text: An `emptyDir` with `sizeLimit: 200Gi`
options.why: emptyDir uses the node's own disk, which is too small here.

options.text: A generic ephemeral volume using the SSD StorageClass
options.why: It provisions a per-Pod PVC from any StorageClass and deletes it with the Pod.

options.text: A shared 200Gi PVC that every batch Pod mounts in turn
options.why: It is not deleted with the Pod and creates contention between Pods.

options.text: A `hostPath` directory sized by the node's kubelet config
options.why: hostPath has no sizing and is limited by the small local disk.

explanation: Generic ephemeral volumes let a Pod request a volume from any StorageClass inline. Kubernetes creates a PVC named `<pod name>-<volume name>` owned by the Pod, so it is provisioned like a normal PVC (network SSD, snapshots, size) but deleted automatically when the Pod is deleted. emptyDir is limited to node-local storage.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Ephemeral Volumes (Generic ephemeral volumes)

stem: A node running a StatefulSet Pod with an RWO volume loses power and will not come back soon. The Pod is stuck Terminating and its replacement cannot attach the volume. Using non-graceful node shutdown handling, put the recovery steps in order.

options.text: Confirm the node is really shut down or unreachable
Add the `node.kubernetes.io/out-of-service` taint to the node
Kubernetes force-deletes the node's Pods and detaches their volumes
The replacement Pod attaches the volume on a healthy node and starts
After the node is recovered, remove the out-of-service taint

explanation: When a node shuts down without the kubelet noticing, StatefulSet Pods stay Terminating and their volumes stay attached, so replacements cannot start. After confirming the node is down, an admin adds the `node.kubernetes.io/out-of-service` taint. Pods without a matching toleration are force-deleted and volume detach happens immediately, letting the replacement attach the volume elsewhere. Remove the taint once the node is repaired.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Node Shutdowns (Non-graceful node shutdown)

stem: A team snapshots a busy MySQL data volume with a VolumeSnapshot every hour. After a restore test, MySQL runs crash recovery and two recent transactions are missing. What explains this?

options.text: Snapshots are crash-consistent; apps must quiesce for a consistent copy
options.why: A snapshot captures the disk at an instant, like after a power cut.

options.text: VolumeSnapshots copy files one by one, so writes in flight are skipped
options.why: Snapshots are block-level and atomic at the storage layer, not file copies.

options.text: The restore PVC was smaller than the original, so the tail was truncated
options.why: A smaller restore size is rejected; it would not silently truncate data.

options.text: Snapshots exclude anything written within the last minute by design
options.why: There is no such exclusion window.

explanation: A CSI VolumeSnapshot captures the volume at a point in time without coordinating with the application, so the result is crash-consistent: like pulling the plug. Databases recover through their write-ahead log, and transactions not yet flushed to disk can be lost. For application-consistent backups, flush and freeze the database first (for example with pre and post hooks in a backup tool), or use the database's own backup tooling.

stem: Which two statements about Velero, a popular Kubernetes backup tool, are accurate? (Choose two.)

options.text: It backs up Kubernetes API objects, such as Deployments and PVCs, to object storage
options.why: Resource manifests are exported and stored in a bucket.

options.text: It can back up volume data via CSI snapshots or a file-system backup
options.why: Velero supports snapshot-based and file-level volume backups.

options.text: It replaces etcd snapshots for recovering the control plane itself
options.why: Velero restores workloads; it is not a control plane disaster-recovery tool.

options.text: It guarantees app-consistent database backups without any hooks
options.why: Consistency for databases still needs hooks or database-native backups.

options.text: It only works on clusters whose StorageClasses use `Retain`
options.why: Reclaim policy has nothing to do with Velero backups.

explanation: Velero backs up cluster resources (exported through the API) to object storage and handles volume data either through snapshots (CSI or provider plugins) or file-system backup with Kopia. Restores can target the same or another cluster, which also makes it useful for migrations. It does not replace etcd backups for control plane recovery, and databases still need hooks or native tools for application-consistent backups.

stem: Pods using `WaitForFirstConsumer` local-disk volumes keep getting scheduled to nodes whose disks are full; provisioning then fails and the scheduler retries elsewhere. Which feature lets the scheduler avoid such nodes up front?

options.text: Raising the Pods' `ephemeral-storage` requests and limits on every container
options.why: Ephemeral-storage requests account for node scratch space, not CSI volume capacity.

options.text: Storage capacity tracking with CSIStorageCapacity objects from the driver
options.why: The scheduler then considers remaining capacity per topology when picking nodes.

options.text: Switching the StorageClass to `volumeBindingMode: Immediate`
options.why: Immediate provisions before scheduling, which makes the mismatch worse for local disks.

options.text: Adding a `nodeSelector` so Pods only land on nodes labelled `disk=free`
options.why: Static labels do not track capacity as it changes.

explanation: With storage capacity tracking, a CSI driver publishes `CSIStorageCapacity` objects that report available capacity per topology segment (such as a node or zone). For volumes with `WaitForFirstConsumer` binding, the scheduler filters out nodes that cannot fit the requested volume, avoiding failed provisioning and retries.

stem: New Pods that each mount several CSI volumes stay `Pending` on a node that has plenty of CPU and memory. Events mention the node exceeding its maximum volume count. Where does the scheduler get that limit?

options.text: From the `maxPods` setting in the kubelet configuration
options.why: maxPods limits Pods per node, not attached volumes.

options.text: From a ResourceQuota on `persistentvolumeclaims` in the Pod's namespace
options.why: Quotas limit how many PVCs a namespace may create, not attachments per node.

options.text: From the CSI driver's allocatable count in the node's CSINode object
options.why: Drivers report how many volumes a node can attach, and the scheduler enforces it.

options.text: From the StorageClass `parameters` field set by the admin
options.why: StorageClass parameters configure provisioning, not per-node attach limits.

explanation: Cloud VMs can attach only a limited number of disks. CSI drivers report the per-node limit through the node plugin, and the kubelet records it as `allocatable.count` for that driver in the node's `CSINode` object. The scheduler counts volumes already attached and refuses nodes that would exceed it, leaving Pods Pending until capacity frees up or a new node is added.

stem: You want to clone the PVC `prod-db` (namespace `prod`) into a PVC in namespace `staging` using `dataSource: {kind: PersistentVolumeClaim, name: prod-db}`. What happens?

options.text: It's rejected: the clone source must be in the destination's namespace
options.why: CSI volume cloning only works within one namespace.

options.text: It works, as long as both PVCs use the same StorageClass
options.why: Even with the same class, cross-namespace cloning is not supported.

options.text: It works, but only while no Pod currently mounts the source PVC prod-db
options.why: Mount state is not the restriction; the namespace boundary is.

options.text: It works, but the clone is read-only until the source is deleted
options.why: Clones are independent writable volumes when supported.

explanation: CSI volume cloning creates a new PVC pre-populated from an existing PVC through `dataSource`. The source must be in the same namespace as the destination, the volume modes must match, and the driver must support cloning. A different StorageClass is allowed. To copy data across namespaces, use a snapshot-based workflow or a backup tool.

stem: Match each symptom with its most likely cause.

options.text: An RWO volume is still attached to another node
options.why: Multi-attach conflict

options.text: The PV is zonal and the Pod is forced into another zone
options.why: Topology conflict

options.text: The filesystem grows only once a Pod mounts the volume
options.why: Offline expansion

options.text: The PVC has no matching PV and no provisioner made one
options.why: Unbound claim

prompts.text: Event: "Multi-Attach error for volume … Volume is already exclusively attached to one node"
Event: "node(s) had volume node affinity conflict"

explanation: These four messages cover most storage incidents. Multi-Attach means an RWO volume is still attached elsewhere (often during a rolling update or after a node failure). A volume node affinity conflict means the PV's topology does not fit the Pod's placement. FileSystemResizePending is an expansion waiting for a mount. Unbound immediate claims mean no PV matched and nothing was dynamically provisioned.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Persistent Volumes; Storage Classes

stem: A Pod writes logs to an `emptyDir` with `sizeLimit: 1Gi` on the node disk. Log rotation breaks and the directory grows to 3Gi. What happens?

options.text: Writes start failing with "no space left on device" as soon as it hits 1Gi
options.why: A disk-backed emptyDir has no hard quota by default; the limit is enforced by eviction.

options.text: The kubelet evicts the Pod once it detects usage above the sizeLimit
options.why: Exceeding the emptyDir sizeLimit is an eviction trigger.

options.text: The container is OOM-killed because emptyDir counts as memory
options.why: Only `medium: Memory` emptyDirs count as memory.

options.text: Nothing happens: sizeLimit is advisory and only used for scheduling
options.why: The kubelet enforces it through local ephemeral storage eviction.

explanation: For a disk-backed emptyDir, `sizeLimit` is enforced through local ephemeral storage management: the kubelet periodically measures usage and evicts the Pod when the volume exceeds its limit. It is not a filesystem quota, so writes keep succeeding until the eviction. For memory-backed emptyDirs, usage counts toward the container memory limit instead.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Volumes (emptyDir); Local ephemeral storage

stem: A StatefulSet `kafka` (3 replicas, template `data`, default retention policy) is deleted. A week later it is recreated with the same name and replicas, but its `volumeClaimTemplates` now set `storageClassName: fast-v2`. Which storage do the Pods `kafka-0` to `kafka-2` get?

options.text: New `fast-v2` volumes, because the template changed and the set is new
options.why: Template changes only matter when a PVC must be created; these PVCs already exist.

options.text: Their old PVCs `data-kafka-0..2` on the old class, with the old data
options.why: The PVCs were retained and match by name, so they are reused.

options.text: The Pods stay Pending because the old PVCs conflict with the new class
options.why: There is no conflict check; existing PVCs with the expected names are simply used.

options.text: Kubernetes migrates the old data onto new `fast-v2` volumes on startup
options.why: Kubernetes never copies data between storage classes.

explanation: With the default `whenDeleted: Retain`, deleting the StatefulSet leaves its PVCs behind. The recreated set looks for PVCs named `data-kafka-<ordinal>`, finds them and mounts them, so the Pods resume with the old data on the old class. The new `storageClassName` only applies to ordinals that have no PVC yet (for example after scaling up). Moving existing replicas to a new class needs new PVCs and a data copy or snapshot restore.
